# McDonald's research study

## What matters

McDonald's combines a restaurant operator, a franchise royalty business and substantial property operations. Looking only at corporate revenue growth misses much of the economic system. In this package's ten-year series, corporate revenue rises from $24.6bn in 2016 to $26.9bn in 2025, while system restaurant sales, derived without counting rent and royalties twice, rise from approximately $85.0bn to $139.4bn. The franchised restaurant share rises from 84.6% to 95.5%. Those shifts materially change reported margins and investment needs. See the [2018 report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/63908/000006390819000010/mcd-12312018x10k.htm), [2021 report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/63908/000006390822000011/mcd-20211231.htm), and [2025 report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/63908/000006390826000035/mcd-20251231.htm).

Franchisee restaurant sales belong to the franchisees. Corporate revenue includes rent, royalties and fees, plus gross sales from company restaurants and other revenue. Conventional franchises typically use property controlled by McDonald's; developmental licensees and affiliates provide more of their own capital. Consequently, a dollar of sales growth in one ownership channel need not produce the same corporate revenue, profit or reinvestment as a dollar in another. The model separates these cohorts and treats its blended fee yields as estimates rather than contractual royalty rates.

Refranchising exchanges gross company revenue for a smaller, higher-margin fee stream. It can raise the reported margin even if the restaurant's economics are unchanged. The China/Hong Kong transaction in 2017 also generated a disposal gain; it should not be projected as recurring organic profit. The [2018 filing](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/63908/000006390819000010/mcd-12312018x10k.htm) explains both the transaction and the revenue presentation effect.

## The latest operating evidence

The [June 2026 filing](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/63908/000006390826000073/mcd-20260630.htm) reports first-half revenue of $13.616bn, GAAP operating income of $6.292bn, CFO of $5.222bn and cash capex of $1.516bn. Global comparable sales growth slowed to 1.3% in Q2; U.S. comparable growth was 0.8%, with negative guest counts partly offset by check growth. Restaurant count reached 46,028, including 44,016 franchised locations. Sales growth is not automatically evidence of stronger traffic or franchisee returns.

The operating opportunity is higher repeat traffic and more efficient restaurants. The valuation risk is paying for upgrades while customer demand and franchisee capacity disappoint. Food, labor, occupancy, promotional intensity and value positioning all matter to franchisees' willingness and ability to reinvest. The package does not claim to have verified a complete franchisee P&L, franchisee debt, or local unit investment schedule.

## September changes the reinvestment case

The [23 September NEXT announcement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/63908/000006390826000076/exhibit991-investorupdate2.htm) sets a 2030 corporate margin ambition in the low-to-mid 50% range, alongside substantial partnering support: approximately $5bn through 2030 and $8.5bn through 2036. Support combines rent relief and capital investment. The 2027–2030 framework includes around $3bn annual baseline capex plus $1.5–2bn cumulative capital partnering. These are future plans, not achieved results.

Our base scenario charges the full announced support, assigns explicit annual timing and includes the remaining spend after 2030. The split and timing are editable assumptions. The model's 2030 core operating margin is approximately 47.5%; the bull case is about 50.1%. Neither is forced to match management's ambition. Restaurant-level efficiency gains principally help franchisees; they cannot simply be multiplied by system sales and added to corporate EBIT.

The unit-growth timetable also changed. The February annual report targeted 50,000 restaurants in 2027; the August quarterly report moved that milestone to 2028. The source-linked chronology preserves both vintages. It does not score a future target as met.

## Property and leases are central

McDonald's retains substantial property investment despite its high franchise mix. Franchise occupancy costs include depreciation and rent paid to landlords. Capital spending therefore cannot be reduced to company-operated restaurant count. The 2025 report disclosed $28.2bn of net PP&E, including $22.8bn used under franchise arrangements. A separate property-value add-on would double count the assets already producing the modeled rent stream unless the operating valuation were carved up consistently.

The [2024 report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/63908/000006390825000012/mcd-20241231.htm) and annual lease disclosures distinguish operating and finance arrangements. The model leaves operating rent in EBIT and does not subtract operating lease liabilities. Finance leased assets are handled as financed investment: their amortization is within D&A, new financed assets are economic capex, and the existing finance liability belongs in the equity bridge. The June interim statement does not provide a verified split of its $14.729bn combined lease liability. Carrying December's $2.352bn finance liability forward as if it were June fact would be false precision.

## Historical comparability and extraction controls

- Ten fiscal years are available, but the underlying business perimeter changed. The series is consolidated and ownership-based rather than a splice of incompatible geographic segments.
- Initial franchise-fee recognition changed under ASC 606 in 2018. Earlier comparative years were not restated. The fee stream is therefore not strictly comparable across that boundary.
- Lease-balance recognition changed under ASC 842. A pre-adoption recognized balance of zero does not mean the business had no lease obligations.
- The pandemic disrupted sales and working-capital timing. The [2020 filing](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/63908/000006390821000013/mcd-20201231.htm) is retained as evidence, rather than treating 2020 as a normal run-rate year.
- Russia disposal and other unusual items affect 2022 reported margins. See the [2022 filing](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/63908/000006390823000012/mcd-20221231.htm). Later ownership transactions and restructuring also affect comparability.
- Other revenue includes technology cost recovery. Giving every incremental dollar a franchise royalty margin would overstate earnings.
- The obvious generic D&A tag captures SG&A only in recent filings. For 2025 it is $457m; consolidated cash-flow D&A is $2.199bn. The latter is the model's starting point.
- Some recent inline/SEC companyfacts weighted-share values are labeled as single shares even though the rendered table is in millions. The history normalizes the display using the filing's unit heading and checks the EPS identity.
- June's primary equity-investment note shows $98m of earnings from the principal investments; the MD&A total for all unconsolidated affiliates is $122m. Both scopes are retained, rather than silently treating them as identical.

## Capital and ownership

June cash is $822m and reported debt is $39.863bn. The quarterly cover gives exactly 707,641,531 common shares at June 30. The H1 diluted EPS denominator is 712.3m weighted shares and is not the same claim count. Cash buybacks were $1.251bn in H1; future buybacks are not a free valuation benefit. Cash spent and the share reduction must be modeled together in any later capital-allocation analysis.

December award disclosures do not establish June award claims. Plan capacity is not an outstanding award, RSUs are not options, and EPS dilution is not a fair-value reserve. The original filing also shows two different option exercise-price figures in different tables; this package leaves that discrepancy unresolved. The 2025 tax note and balance-sheet long-term tax amounts also require reconciliation before a detailed claim reserve is admitted. Both issues are explicitly documented in `capital-claims-scope-v2.json`.

Negative book equity is not itself evidence that the franchise has no economic value, nor a sensible denominator for a mechanical ROE-derived terminal assumption. The model's terminal incremental ROIC is an explicit analyst assumption.

## What is ready, and what is not

The operating evidence and scenario engine are ready for independent review. They are not a current trading recommendation. Default per-share output remains unavailable until finance-lease, affiliate ownership, existing-award and other capital claims are explicitly resolved or deliberately assumed. There is no verified current price, no current upside, no post-June capital roll-forward and no certified debt-refinancing or dividend/buyback funding model.

## Observed distributions and financing scope

H1 2026 CFO less cash capex was $3.706bn, compared with $3.891bn of dividends and buybacks, a $185m deficit before other investing, financing and FX flows. The corresponding FY2025 surplus was only $15m. This limited comparison is neither FCFF nor a solvency forecast. [June cash flows](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/63908/000006390826000073/mcd-20260630.htm), [annual cash flows](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/63908/000006390826000035/mcd-20251231.htm).

The annual debt note reports no 2026 maturities after classification adjustments, including approximately $1.5bn of short-term obligations supported by the credit line expiring June 2028. The exact components are $798m short-term borrowings and $725m current maturities, already included in reported debt. Zero in that maturity bucket does not establish no near-term financing dependence, and those amounts must not be added to debt twice. [Annual debt financing note](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/63908/000006390826000035/mcd-20251231.htm).
